To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the average carbon footprint is 7.2 tCO2e/cap/y (range 0.9-29.6) and that the average footprint is 4.2 tCO 2e/cap/yr (range 0-10) for CO2 only, with a cross-country expenditure elasticity of 0.57 (0.81 for CO2 only).

(1) 72% of GHG-emissions are related to household and government consumption, (2) 20% are related to food, 19% to operation and maintenance of dwellings, and 17% to mobility, (3) the expenditure elasticity for GHG-emissions on a global level is 0.56, (4) the expenditure elasticity is 1 for CO2 emissions, (5) food is more important in poor countries and mobility in rich countries,
The carbon footprint of nations is strongly linked to consumption expenditure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new and important aspect of the global carbon cycle, the human dimension.
how much greenhouse gas emission a country's citizens cause, not where the emissions occur.
the carbon footprint of nations and how it is linked to the global economy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

consumption is a key determinant of GHG emissions and hence climate change, and that consumption-related GHG emissions are highly unevenly distributed across nations and within nations, with the highest per capita emissions in rich nations and the highest absolute emissions in poor nations.
the carbon footprint of nations is a function of income, population, and the structure of final consumption.
consumption is responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the carbon footprint of nations depends on their consumption patterns and their level of development.
the carbon footprint of nations can be understood in terms of the consumption categories and their relative importance.
GHG emission reduction policies should be designed with a focus on the final consumer, rather than the producer, and with a focus on consumption categories, rather than on technologies or sectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global GHG emissions are not just an aggregate of national emissions but a result of global trade and consumption.
a global carbon price is not a sufficient policy instrument, because the carbon content of goods and services is unevenly distributed.
a global perspective on greenhouse gas emissions, including trade, is essential for understanding the drivers of GHG emissions and their mitigation.
